title: Prevalence of depression and dementia among institutionalized elderly in Kenya: Nairobi county
abstract: Objective The purpose of this investigation was to determine the prevalence of and the link between depression and dementia, and other risk factors among institutionalized elderly in Kenya. Methods This research utilized a cross-sectional design. The sample of 194 was selected through simple random sampling. This study used 6-Item Cognitive Impairment test (6-CIT), Geriatric Depression Scale (GDS) and the Cornell Scale for Depression in Dementia (CSDD) to measure the point prevalence of depression and dementia, and a socio-demographic questionnaire to explore the other objectives. Results 11% and 37% screened positive for depression and dementia respectively. Identified risk factors for institutionalization were: being single, having an impairment, chronic illness, poor self-rated health, being dependent for basic daily functioning and having little social support. This study observed a positive relationship between depression and dementia ( r = .253, df = 186, p < .001). There was a statistically significant relationships between having supportive family and dementia ( r = -.181, N = 191, p = .012); and being dependent for basic daily functioning to both depression ( r = .191, N = 191, p = .008) and dementia ( r = .221, N = 191, p = .002). Conclusion Institutionalized elderly had a higher prevalence for depression and dementia. Being married and having higher levels of education were noted to be important protective factors against dementia. Overall study findings indicate that older adult’s mental health may be associated with multiple levels of factors including stressors and resources concurrently, which makes it imperative to further examine these relationships methodically.
